title: What isn't brain? Artifacts
objective: Recognize the most common EEG artifacts by their shape, timing, and location on the scalp, and explain why a BCI must not mistake them for brain activity.

blocks.text: Brain signals are only microvolts. A single blink can be ten times bigger. How do you tell what came from the brain?

blocks.markdown:
## Not everything on an EEG is brain

An **artifact** is any part of a recording that did not come from the brain. Because brain signals are so small, almost anything electrical near the electrodes can swamp them.

Artifacts come from two places:

- **Your body**: eyes, muscles, and heart all produce electrical fields of their own
- **Your equipment and surroundings**: loose electrodes, cables, and building wiring

## Artifacts from the body

**Eye blinks.** The eyeball is an electrical dipole: the front (cornea) is positive relative to the back (retina). Each blink shifts that dipole, producing a large, slow hump that is biggest on the forehead channels (**Fp1**, **Fp2**) and fades toward the back of the head.

**Muscle tension (EMG).** Muscle fibres fire much faster than cortex, so clenching the jaw or frowning adds dense, fast “fuzz”. It is strongest on the temporal channels (**T7**, **T8**), which sit over the jaw muscles.

**Heartbeat (ECG).** The heart is the strongest electrical generator in the body. Its field can reach the scalp as sharp, evenly spaced spikes about once a second.

## Artifacts from equipment

**Mains interference.** Building wiring carries alternating current at **60 Hz** in North America (50 Hz in much of the world). It shows up as a perfectly regular oscillation with the same strength on every channel.

**A loose electrode.** When an electrode loses contact, its voltage jumps suddenly. Real brain activity is spread across neighbouring electrodes, so a jump on one channel alone is a warning sign.

## Why this matters for BCIs

Researchers handle artifacts by **rejecting** bad stretches of data, **filtering** (for example, a notch filter at 60 Hz), or separating sources with techniques like **independent component analysis**. None of these work unless someone first recognizes what they are looking at.

blocks.text: A BCI that “reads concentration” may actually be reading your forehead muscles. If people frown when they focus, a decoder can learn the frown. Always check what a model is really responding to.

blocks.markdown:
## Your turn

Each round shows 6 seconds of 12-channel EEG. Find the clue, name the cause, and remember the last round may have nothing wrong at all.

blocks.text: These traces are generated by the app, not recorded from a real person. Each artifact is modelled on how it is produced, with amplitudes and timing in typical physiological ranges, so you can practise the patterns safely.

blocks.goal: Identify the source of contamination in six EEG recordings, including one that is clean.

items.prompt: A large, slow hump appears on Fp1 and Fp2 and fades toward the back of the head. What is the most likely cause?
items.explain: Blinks move the eye’s electrical dipole. The forehead electrodes, closest to the eyes, see the biggest deflection.

items.prompt: A regular 60 Hz oscillation has the same strength on every channel. Where does it most likely come from?
items.explain: Building wiring radiates a 60 Hz field that every electrode picks up equally. No brain rhythm is identical on every channel.

choices.text: The heart, which beats about 60 times a minute

items.prompt: C4 suddenly jumps to a new level, but its neighbours do not change. What should you suspect first?
items.explain: Brain activity spreads across neighbouring electrodes. A jump confined to one channel points to a contact or hardware problem.

choices.text: A burst of activity in the right motor cortex

items.prompt: A “focus” headset works well, and users frown when they concentrate. What is the biggest concern?
items.explain: Forehead and jaw muscle activity is much larger than brain signals. The decoder may be detecting the frown, not the focus.

choices.text: It may be detecting muscle activity instead of brain activity
Frowning makes the brain signal stronger, so it is more accurate
Nothing, as long as the accuracy is high
